 The sun powers our world, and with the right portable solar panel, it can also power your outdoor adventures or home emergency set up. I’ve tested dozens of models from top brands like Bluetti, Jackery, Anker, Goal Zero, EcoFlow, and BioLite, and have come away impressed with their power generation potential. To help you decide which of the best portable solar panels is right for you, I tested 14 options running from 100W to 400W for power potential, ease of use, and portability.

 If you’re looking to purchase both a power station and portable solar panel, check out my take on the best solar generators ; It looks at which pairings provide the best bang for your buck. 
 How I Tested the Best Portable Solar Panels
 My portable solar panel testing consisted of three criteria: performance (measured power output), portability, and ease of use. I also considered other factors like price, warranty, and IP rating (a third-party test that looks at dustproofness and waterproofness). I focused this review on the portable solar panels between 100W and 400W and tested panels from Jackery, Bluetti, EcoFlow, Anker, Goal Zero, Dakota Lithium, Vtoman, Zendure, Ugreen, BioLite, and Lion Energy. If you are looking for a smaller panel that you can connect directly to a phone, check out our test of the best solar chargers . 
 Testing Power Generation 
 Performance was tested twice: on a clear day and on a cloudy day. I used the best portable power stations to measure the solar energy generated by each panel and used an older version of the Anker SOLIX 100W panel as my control panel to account for inconsistent conditions between tests. I used the attached sundial on the Anker SOLIX 100W (not included in newer models, unfortunately) to ensure the panels were always optimally oriented toward the sun. Then I took a reading from each panel, adjusting the results as necessary based on the reading of the control panel. 
 Testing the Portable Solar Panels’ Ease of Use
 Ease of use was assessed by looking at how easy or difficult it was to set up each panel. Some portable solar panels had adjustable legs or sundials that made them quick and easy to use —- these were ranked as Excellent. Others toppled over easily, refused to lie flat, or had complicated setups. Those were rated Poor. 
 Testing Portability 
 How portable a solar panel is depends in large part on its physical size. 400W portable solar panels are a lot harder to lug around than 100W portable solar panels, and they won’t fit as easily in your car or on a garage shelf. Even given that, I was surprised at how much variability there is in features such as handles, cable storage, and latching mechanisms. I moved each portable solar panel up and down multiple flights of stairs and out to my testing site over several days, giving me ample insight into how portable each unit is. 
 Grading
 While the above criteria is how I graded each of the best portable solar panels, there is one more factor that should inform your choice: compatibility with your portable power station . There are two things you need to check: load compatibility and port compatibility. For load compatibility, check that both the volts and the wattage supplied by the portable solar panel won’t overload your power station. I’ve listed the specs for each portable solar panel in this test, and you can typically find the information for your power station in very small font on the bottom of the unit. 
 For port compatibility, you simply want to look at whether the cord coming out of the portable solar panel can be connected to the power station you are purchasing. Unfortunately, different brands use different cords, and some brands even use different cords within their lineup, which is all very frustrating. In some instances, you may be able to purchase an adapter cord if the provided cable for the portable solar panel doesn’t match the ports on your power station. Goal Zero has a number of cables to convert mismatched ports and plugs that can help get you started.
 Updates
 Previously, I had recommended the Anker SOLIX 100W as my best value pick in the 100-watt category. That was in large part due to its built-in sundial, which is invaluable in maximizing the power generation potential of the best portable solar panels. Unfortunately, Anker has since removed the sundial feature from the updated panel. I’ll be testing their new 100-watt panel in coming weeks and will provide an update on its performance at that time.

And in its size category, the Bluetti PV120 is far and away the best performer, producing well over 100 watts in full sun while beating out the competition in shady conditions. It’s exceptionally portable, with a comfortable handle, an accordion shape that clips together so it won’t come apart while you’re walking. I also appreciate the handy storage bag for its cable, so that you don’t misplace it when not in use. Trust me, I misplaced plenty of charging cables while testing the best portable solar panels and being able to pack away the charging cable with the solar panel itself is very helpful. 
 The smaller sized portable solar panels are all easier to set up than the larger 200W and 400W models, but even within these, the Bluetti PV120 stood out as being easy to use. It’s plenty easy to set up; It’s plenty easy to transport. It’s the total package. The carrying case design is also top notch, with a comfortable handle and zippered pouch for its cable. The snaps that hold the panels in place when folded up are also a nice tough.
 Details like adjustable legs, a zippered pouch for cords, and clasps to hold the panel while in transit make the Bluetti PV200 a joy to use.  
 I don’t love the warranty on this — one year is awfully short or a product that realistically should last a decade or more. But that’s my only gripe. After a year of using and abusing the 120W version of this panel, I haven’t run into any durability issues with this series yet.

 Watt for watt, the Zendure 400W solar panel has exceptionally good performance. In ideal weather conditions, I’ve seen it generate over 400 watts of power at a time. It’s also surprisingly lightweight, easy to transport, and, for a larger portable solar panel, wasn’t particularly onerous to set up. I did not, however, keep it in my arsenal after my initial test (in conjunction with my appraisal of the Zendure SuperBase) due to its large size and lack of compatibility, and thus was unable to perform a test in cloudy weather conditions. 
 It was easier than I expected to adjust the legs of the Zendure 400W solar panel. 
 The Zendure 400W comes with an XT-90 cable. That means it’s not compatible with any power station in my test of the best portable power stations; in fact, the only power station I’ve ever tested that it is compatible with is the Zendure SuperBase, a power station that was not what I would call “portable,” given that it weighed nearly as much as I do. While the stated voltage output of the Zendure 400W is such that it should be possible to convert it to a different connector style (like an XT-60) with an adaptor, I have not tested this so cannot speak to whether a loss in amps would affect the power output potential. 
 The other catch to the Zendure 400W is that it’s pricey, a whopping $500 more than my best value pick.

 This one was closer than I was expecting. The Vtoman 400W solar panel, despite being heavier, was easier to transport due to its better handle design and the zip pocket for the cable. It also had a better performance in cloudy weather than the Anker SOLIX 400W.
 A look at the adjustable kickstand legs of the Anker SOLIX 400W
 But the Anker SOLIX 400W had a strong showing in full sun, was a couple hundred dollars less expensive, and was miles easier to set up. The Vtoman 400W has floppy kickstand legs that are difficult to get into position. The Anker SOLIX 400W has adjustable legs that made it fairly simple to get what would otherwise be an unwieldy panel set to the right angle for optimal power generation. Given how important it is to adjust the angle of your portable solar panel regularly to maximize power potential, this is an important detail that puts the Anker SOLIX in the top spot for value. 
 The Rest of the Field
 While the Vtoman 400W solar panel had one of the worst setups of any portable solar panel I tested (giant panel plus floppy legs is a bad combo), it did come with my all-time favorite cable. This one can be paired, out of the box, with the widest array of power stations. While there is some danger with mixing and matching portable solar panels and power stations (Goal Zero has told me that they discourage it with their products), for individuals confident that they can assess the power potential and capabilities of various power stations, this could be an interesting choice. 
 The excellent cable set up of the Vtoman 400W solar panel 
 While I’m a big fan of EcoFlow’s portable power stations (their Delta 2 was my best overall pick in that test ), I find their portable solar panels unnecessarily fussy. First off, they don’t have kickstands. Instead you’re meant to attach the panel to the four corners of the carrying case, and then adjust the angle by zipping or unzipping the case. This more or less works, but is ridiculously fiddly. 
 Second, this panel, when stored for long periods of time, can start to warp such that I have found it difficult to fully flatten out. As a result, I think you’re better off skipping these units, despite their impressive power potential. The only exception to this is if you are specifically looking for a panel that can generate power on both sides — in my testing, it typically can produce half the volume of power on the opposite side, which is an interesting feature. 
 Proper setup of EcoFlows solar panels is generally more of a pain than I’m willing to deal with.  
 I similarly find there to be a pretty major discrepancy between my experience of Goal Zero’s portable power stations and their portable solar panels. Their Boulder series, while somewhat more affordable, is heavy and clunky for the amount of power it produces and you can’t adjust the angle to match the sun. I was optimistic that the more lightweight Nomad 200W would improve on the experience but I was, unfortunately, unable to complete testing due to the incompatibility of its charging cables with the Goal Zero unit I have on hand. 
 While the cloudy weather testing result was quite impressive, the sun has disappeared from these PNW skies for the foreseeable future (I will update this review with the results of the blue sky testing at a later date). Also frustrating was the lack of a carrying handle on the case, a detail that made it surprisingly awkward to carry. When I queried Goal Zero, they reported that their portable solar panels will operate down to -40° F, far and away the lowest claimed temperature in my test. 
 The Dakota Lithium 180 got surprisingly high marks for portability but was ultimately not powerful enough compared to other panels at that price point and lower. It also eschewed kickstands in favor of tie-off loops which was fine, but I would have preferred the kickstands to achieve maximum solar input. But the unique accordion shape of the panel made it, by far, the most portable solar panel in my test.
 The Lion Energy 100W 12V solar panel very nearly made the cut. It’s definitely worth a look if you are planning to pair it with one of Lion Energy’s portable power stations.  
 A few panels that impressed on portability and ease of use but failed to deliver the power others were capable of included the BioLite 100W, and the Ugreen 100W. The Lion Energy did impress during testing (it also stood out as one of the few portable solar panels that didn’t look like it had been produced in a mono manufacturing facility), but didn’t quite make the cut for one of the above awards.

While there are some solar chargers that include ports for a classic USB-A or USB-C cable, the ones in this test are producing so much power that this is not an effective way to capture it — if they went full throttle at your phone they would fry it. So you need an intermediary to hold the power and release it in a controlled way.
 I needed two different power stations to test portable solar panels from Anker and Lion Energy, because their solar panel connector types made it difficult to mix and match.  Laura Lancaster 
 There are two specs to check for when looking to see if your portable solar panel is compatible with your portable power station: power potential and connector/port compatibility. 
 Power Potential Compatibility
 Portable solar panels aren’t all that smart. Whatever blast of sun they are getting will be transmitted directly as power to your power station. So before you purchase a portable solar panel, first look at your power station to see how much solar input it can handle. (This is typically found in very small font on the bottom of your power station). Don’t purchase a portable solar panel or solar panels that exceeds this power potential, as it can damage the battery in your power station.
 Portable Solar Panel Connector and Power Station Port Compatibility
 In the same way that you can’t plug a USB-C charging cord into a lightning port, not all portable solar panel cable connectors are compatible with every power station port. The most common ones I’ve seen while testing are 8mm DC, XT60, HPP (High Power Port). While you can in some cases find an adaptor cord so that you can use a portable solar panel with an 8mm charging cable with a power station with an XT60 port, this is a bit of pain.
 Power Potential of the Best Portable Solar Panels
 Once you’ve locked in on which portable solar panels are compatible with your current power station, the next major question to ask is how much power you want to generate. Generally, larger portable solar panels generate more power than smaller portable solar panels, but are unwieldy to transport and set up. The above tables drill down more on which portable solar panels in testing produced the most power in full sun.
 Portability and Ease of Set Up of the Best Portable Solar Panels
 While several of the portable solar panels I tested seemed to be made in the same manufacturing plant — same colors and fabrics, similar design choices — there was still some surprising variability in ease of set up and portability. Generally, the largest portable solar panels were the most difficult to move and set up, and the smaller ones the easiest, but details like handle comfort and number of kickstands made a surprising difference in the overall experience.
 FAQs
 Q: Is it worth getting a portable solar panel? It’s a lot of fun to own a portable solar panel. Charging up your phone or your laptop with nothing more than the power of the sun is pretty satisfying, and it can give you some peace of mind in the event of a power outage. For some people, it can supplement one of the best portable power stations as part of their at-home emergency kits. For others, it can extend the length of time they are able to be off-grid with an overlanding setup. Typically, though, whether or not a portable solar panel is worth it depends in large part on how much sun the area you are in gets. 
 Q: How much energy can a portable solar panel produce? I was impressed to see that the best portable solar panels really do produce the amount of power they say they do. If you live in a sunny part of the country, you can be confident that the wattage stated on the portable solar panel is more or less the wattage that you will get — assuming you get the panel oriented for optimal efficiency. I recommend purchasing a sundial to clip onto your portable solar panel so that you can be sure it’s angled directly at the sun.  
 Q: What size portable solar panel do I need? The size portable solar panel you need depends on a few factors, including how much energy your power station can accept from a portable solar panel, how much power you are hoping to generate, and how important portability is to you. 
 Final Thoughts on the Best Portable Solar Panels
 The best portable solar panels on this list are all excellent choices for pairing with the best portable power stations. If you do decide to mix and match brands and models, double check that the cable requirements and voltage capabilities match up first.

 The right solar panel setup will seriously boost the power in your adventure rig.   Credit: Chris McNamara 
 How We Tested
 Since 2011, we have researched, purchased, and tested dozens of portable solar panels for camping. Our rigorous side-by-side tests pit these sun-gathering machines against each other. Much of our testing involved measuring how quickly each solar panel charged a battery at the same location and time to ensure the most accurate results. We connected each solar panel to a matching battery simultaneously to ensure identical conditions, then recorded the charge each panel generated in two hours. 
 Our testing of these solar panels is divided into three rating metrics with weights corresponding to their overall importance: 
 Power Efficiency (60% of overall weighting) 
 Portability (20% of overall weighting) 
 Ease of Setup (20% of overall weighting) 
 Why Trust GearLab
 Our expert panel review team is led by Kenji Mowrey . Kenji has been a Review Editor at GearLab for three years. He tests power stations for Gear Lab, so it only makes sense to have him lead the testing for solar panels as well. Kenji is passionate about running, biking, and camping. He holds a bachelor's degree in Outdoor Product Design from Oregon State and draws on his camping experience and knack for design to understand what makes a great solar panel. 
 Sam Schild also lent his expertise and writing abilities in putting together this review. Sam is an avid outdoorsy person who has spent countless nights camping miles away from the nearest electrical outlet. He first used a solar panel during a cross-country bicycle tour in 2012 to power his cell phone. He currently lives full-time in a campervan with 300 watts of solar panels attached to the roof for power. 
 Previous Next 
 We tested these panels side-by-side to ensure consistent conditions and get reliable results.
 Analysis and Test Results
 Worse Value
 Better Value
 What's the Best Value?
 Price doesn't always equal performance in this category. Several of the most expensive panels we tested underperformed in efficiency and other key areas. Some of our top-rated panels were also among the best values. Keep in mind that price per watt depends on current sales. For the best energy output per dollar, divide the lowest price you can find by our “ Measured Watts ” (listed below in the review text and above in the specs).
 The Renogy 200W Portable is our top overall pick and offers the best value among the portable solar panels we tested for camping and off-grid use. If it had not won Editors' Choice, it would have won Best Buy. While not the cheapest option, it delivers consistently excellent performance and efficiency. And it costs hundreds less than many other models. 
 It's worth paying a few extra bucks for the Renogy 200W Portable panel because it's efficient and very portable.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W is one of the least expensive panels we tested that still works well. This panel doesn't fold, so it isn't the best for every use case, but if you're looking for an inexpensive panel to mount on your roof, whether that's a moving or fixed roof, this is a great option that won't break the bank. We have also seen some RV users buy inexpensive generic stands for using this panel on the ground. It is heavier and bulkier than the foldable options in this review, but with the right support, it can be made pretty sturdy and wind-resistant.
 The FlexSolar 100W costs less than every other panel in this review. But this model is only 100 watts, whereas most of the other panels here are 200 watts. So while the FlexSolar is the least expensive, it isn't the least expensive per watt —that award goes to the JJn Bifacial 200W . 
 In the chart below, we show the cost per watt for each panel. We calculate this by dividing the price by the actual efficiency we measured in testing, rather than the manufacturer's claimed rating.
 The Marbero 200W Portable is also very inexpensive, making it a great value for a folding 200-watt solar panel. However, this panel's measured watt output is only 134 watts. So, the cost per watt of this panel is $1.32, which is more than the JJN and the FlexSolar . You may be paying less for this panel, but you are also getting less power than expected.
 You'll pay a low cost per watt for the JJN Bifacial 200W, and we're talking measured watts here.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W produced the most raw output of any panel in our lineup at 193 measured watts. This panel regularly sells for 40-50% off MSRP, and this “ street price ” is a great value. 
 We've never actually seen the EcoFlow NextGen 220W sold for its MSRP, so be sure to buy this one when it's discounted.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible is the best value for van lifers and overlanders who want to mount a panel on top of their rig. It's one of the lightest panels we tested, is pretty efficient overall, and only requires industrial adhesive or double-stick tape to mount—no drilling or extra hardware required. This saves you money and time. 
 Power Efficiency
 The main use of a large solar panel is to convert sunlight into energy, so we weighted this metric heavily. If a panel doesn't reliably generate power, then it isn't worth the investment, no matter how portable or easy to set up it might be. 
 We used two measured results to assess power efficiency: the number of watts charged in 2 hours of direct sunlight, and the percent of the claimed power (in watts) actually delivered when charging a power station. A 100% efficient system using a 200-watt panel would charge 200 watt-hours in each hour of direct sun, but how efficient is each of these systems?
 We connected each panel to an identical Jackery portable power station to test charging capabilities.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 To test power efficiency, we connected each panel to a Jackery 1000 power station (1070Wh capacity). We then let the panels charge their respective battery for two hours and calculated the total watt-hours generated. During the test, we recorded the input power every 30 minutes to calculate the actual output power relative to each panel's claimed wattage. 
 We performed these power-efficiency tests at an elevation of 6300 feet on a clear day. The temperature was between 55 and 65° F.
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W generated the most charge over our two-hour test. This panel generated 385 watts over the test period, for a measured power of 193 watts per hour. If this panel were 200 watts like most of the rest of the test lineup, that would be extremely efficient. As it is, though, this panel remains very efficient and generated the most power during our tests. If you're going by looks, this panel is about the same size as the other folding models, though. So the fact that it's technically less efficient because it's 20 watts more than the competition is kind of a moot point. 
 The EcoFlow NextGen is technically a 220-watt panel, while most of the other models we tested are 200 watts.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W generated 182 watts per hour, charging its 1070-watt-hour test battery a whopping 34% in two hours. Input readings were consistently between 194 and 200 watts throughout our two-hour test. Its bifacial cell design, which captures light on both sides of the panel, almost certainly contributes to this exceptional performance. And 182 watts in an hour is 91% of the 200 watts this panel is rated for. That's super efficient. 
 If you needed to fully charge a 1000-watt-hour battery, which is a common size for a power station, you could do that with either the EcoFlow NextGen or the JJN Bifacial in about 6 hours. That's some serious power. 
 The next most efficient solar panel is the Renogy 200W Portable . This panel generated 177 watts in an hour. You could also theoretically charge a 1000-watt-hour battery from 0 to 100% in about 6 hours with this model. And since it's a 200W panel, its measured efficiency is higher than the EcoFlow NextGen 's, too. 
 Just behind those panels is the Jackery SolarSaga 200 . This panel produced 171 watts per hour at 86% efficiency. This is one of the most consistent foldable panels in our test lineup.
 Elevation, air temperature, and the surface you set your panel on can all affect a solar panel's energy output. We've found that hotter weather and lower elevations reduce solar panel efficiency. Laying your panel directly on a hot surface, such as blacktop or the roof of your house, will reduce efficiency, especially if the battery is also on that same surface. Instead, prop your panel up on its kickstand legs to create airflow below, which will keep it cooler and boost efficiency. 
 The next highest-scoring panels in power efficiency were the BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible , Anker Solix PS200 , and Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase . Each of these panels charged its test battery to 31% in two hours.
 The Anker Solix charged our test battery almost as efficiently as the top-performing panels.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 Portability
 While not as important as power efficiency, portability is also a consideration when choosing a solar panel. 
 We tested portability by weighing each model with a scale in our test lab. We also measured the size of each panel when folded and when opened. Most of the models we tested here are designed to be packed into your trunk and set up wherever you need them. So, we also assessed how easy it was to transport these panels throughout the test period. We paid special attention to features that made carrying them easier, such as ergonomic handles, cable storage, and carrying cases. 
 Most of the panels we tested have carrying handles, which made weighing them on our test lab's luggage scale a cinch.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The easiest panel to carry is the FlexSolar 100W . This panel weighs only 4.1 pounds and folds down to the size of a laptop. Most of the other panels we tested are 200 watts, and more surface area is required for more watts. But even the 100-watt versions of these other panels are still larger and heavier than the FlexSolar 100W. 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible is the lightest 200-watt panel we tested. This model only weighs 6.6 pounds. That's over twice as light as the next most portable 200-watt model. 
 The Arch doesn't fold, though, and doesn't have carrying handles or a place to stash cables. It's designed to be mounted on a fiberglass van roof, a boat, a hardshell rooftop tent, or another surface without weighing it down. So even though this panel is significantly lighter than most folding models, we wouldn't necessarily choose it for a panel to pack in the trunk with your camping gear.
 The lightest foldable 200-watt panels are the Jackery SolarSaga 200 (14.2 lbs), Marbero 200W Portable (14.2 lbs), and Renogy 200W Portable (14.8 lbs). These panels fold down to a smaller size than the BougeRV Arch . And even though they weigh over twice as much, they're easier to carry and pack in a trunk because they have a handle and fold. 
 The Renogy 200W Portable has a zippered pocket large enough to store a phone or small accessories along with the integrated charging cables. This makes it easier to pack and stay organized, despite the extra half-pound of weight compared to the Marbero and Jackery. 
 The EcoFlow NextGen is one of the few folding panels with a separate carrying case, which you may or may not prefer.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W weighs 16.5 lbs and comes with a carrying case to protect the panel during transport. This is useful, but if you lose the case, the panel becomes much harder to carry. For this reason, we prefer built-in handles to a separate case. But you might feel differently. 
 The Anker Solix PS200 (17.1 lbs) and Grecell 200W Portable (17.3 lbs) are comparable in terms of portability. The Anker uses snap buttons to keep it folded up during transport. The Grecell has a cable storage bag and two clips to prevent it from unfolding. 
 The ZOUPW 200W Foldable (18.3 lbs) and Bluetti 200W Portable (18.9 lbs) are on the heavier side for folding 200W panels. You can still carry either of these on your own, but the extra weight is noticeable compared to the lighter models listed above.
 Technically, the Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase is portable, but you won't want to carry it far.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase , at 43.3 lbs, is the least portable panel we tested. The fact that it has a carrying handle and a carrying case is helpful in some ways, but many people will still find it too heavy to carry on their own. We'd prefer to have a friend help carry it, and it's much easier to fit it into the carrying bag with help, too. This panel is best for setting up in a location and leaving it there, so the fact that it even has a handle feels wrong. 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W , on the other hand, doesn't try to be portable. At 25 lbs, this panel weighs significantly less than the Goal Zero Briefcase. But it doesn't fold or have a carrying handle. This is also better for setting up in a location and not moving it ever again, unless it's attached to the roof of a vehicle. 
 By measuring both weight and ease of transport, we arrived at our overall portability score.
 We wouldn't recommend loading the JJN Bifacial into the trunk of your car as we did.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 Ease of Setup
 A portable solar panel that is hard to set up defeats the purpose of it being portable. When you're camping, you don't want to spend hours setting up solar panels; you want to enjoy nature, right?
 We evaluated ease of setup by timing how long it took us to set up each panel. Setup time for each panel varied widely — it ranged from 31 seconds to 10 minutes! 
 We also used qualitative ratings based on what makes it easier or harder to start charging with these panels. We looked at how the kickstand legs worked, how much you could adjust the angle, built-in cable storage options, wind stability, and more. 
 The amount of time it takes to set up a portable solar panel controls how quickly you can relax at camp.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Renogy 200W Portable was the easiest to set up overall. It sets up in just 35 seconds, so you can start charging shortly after getting to camp. And once you've set this panel up, it's sturdier than other portable solar panels. While its kickstand legs look similar to those of other budget folding panels, they are larger and sturdier. This panel is more wind-resistant than other folding models we tested, especially when you use stakes to secure the legs. It also has a zippered pouch for storing cables when you're not using them, which keeps things much tidier in a packed trunk. 
 The Jackery SolarSaga 200 is also very easy to set up. We had this panel upright and charging in 35 seconds. It has kickstand legs that deploy quickly, and the magnetic closure on the handle opens easily when you want it to, not when you don't. The charging cable has an 8 mm DC connector, which pairs perfectly with the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 models we used for testing. If you're trying to use this panel with a different power station brand, you'll likely need to buy a common adaptor. Some panels come with several adaptors so they can easily attach to any power station battery, but not this one. 
 The Grecell 200W Portable went from folded to charging in 31 seconds, the shortest time of any model. This panel also comes with MC4 power cables with four different connector types, so it can connect to any power station without requiring you to purchase the correct adaptor. However, after the testing period, the stitching on the canvas covering the panel is already beginning to separate. This makes us skeptical about how long it will last. 
 The Goal Zero Boulder Briefcase took longer to set up than most of the other folding panels we tested.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Anker Solix PS200 set up in 43 seconds, which is still quite fast, albeit not quite the fastest. But this panel has tons of other useful features. The kickstand legs have snap buttons to adjust the angle. Each leg has four different attachment points at 30, 40, 50, and 80 degrees. Since the legs are on the longer side, it takes a bit of maneuvering to keep them spread out when setting up with one person. But this also makes the panel more stable once you've set it up. It has MC4 connector cables, but they're shorter than most other panels. For long-term use, we recommend getting an extension cable.
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible and JJN Bifacial 200W are also notable in this category. They take much longer to set up than the folding models. The BougeRV takes 400 seconds, and the JJN 600 seconds. However, neither of these panels needs to be taken down once you've attached them to the roof of your vehicle, so technically the setup time is zero seconds after the initial setup. But, mounting these panels requires some hardware and mechanical know-how. So if you aren't looking to install a panel on your vehicle's roof, you should opt for a folding, portable solar panel. 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible requires no setup time once you've mounted it to the roof of your vehicle.   Credit: Sam Schild 
 Conclusion
 Choosing the right portable solar panel for your camping setup can feel daunting. Making the correct purchase can be the difference between a panel that lasts a long time and one that leaves you short on charge in the backcountry. Now that we've given you our take on the best large solar panels, hopefully you can make the right purchasing decision for your needs. 
 Hopefully, this guide brings you to beautiful places with plenty of power for all your tech.   Credit: Sam Schild

The listing rates it IP67 waterproof and hail-resistant, so rain and light hail are part of its intended use, though the connectors should not be submerged.  Compatibility is the main trade-off. The MC4 output cables work with listed Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and BLUETTI models, but the 4-in-1 adapter cable is sold separately , and 12V/24V battery systems need a charge controller that is not included.  FAQs
 Can a 400W portable solar panel charge a power station directly?
 It can when the panel’s voltage and connector match your station’s input, which is the detail that trips up most buyers. A panel rated near 47V open circuit will not work with a small station limited to 30V, so check your model’s maximum input before ordering. Most kits here include MC4 to XT60, Anderson, or DC8020 adapters.
 How much does a 400W portable solar panel actually weigh?
 Folded panels in this class run roughly 20 to 31 pounds, and that spread decides how often you bother setting one up. A 20-pound suitcase is manageable for one person over a short walk from the vehicle. Heavier fiberglass-backed models suit basecamp setups where the panel stays put for days.
 Do you need a charge controller with a portable solar panel?
 You need one when charging a bare 12V or 24V battery, but not when plugging into a power station that already regulates input. Panels with MC4 output feed a compatible controller directly. For a station, the built-in MPPT handles regulation, so adding a second controller just introduces another failure point.
 Is a bifacial panel worth it for camping?
 Bifacial panels earn their keep on sand, snow, or pale concrete where reflected light hits the rear face, adding up to about 10 percent more output. On grass or forest duff the gain shrinks. If you camp mostly on dirt and shade, a standard single-sided panel at a lower weight is the more practical choice.
 Final Thoughts
 The deciding factors in this category are voltage compatibility, folded weight, and how quickly you can re-aim the panel as the sun moves. Get those three right and a 400W panel will refill a mid-size power station over a clear day, even if clouds trim the output. Get them wrong and you own an expensive folding table.
 For most campers and van setups, the 400W Portable Solar Panel for Power Station is the pick I would start with. At 20.3 pounds it is the easiest to carry of the group, the six-angle kickstand lets you chase the sun without dragging the whole panel, and the included MC4 to XT60, Anderson, and DC8020 cables cover the common power station ports. Skip it if you run a large 2kWh station that wants higher voltage headroom, or if you need a panel that stays mounted on a roof full time. For everyone else, check the current price on Amazon and confirm your station’s input voltage first, which is the one spec that decides whether any of this works.

 Your Power Station Is Only Half the Equation
 A portable power station without solar panels is a very expensive battery. It charges once from the wall, you drain it, and then you're stuck waiting for grid power to come back. That's fine for a 4-hour outage. It's a problem for a 3-day hurricane recovery, a week-long camping trip, or a season of tailgating.
 Solar panels turn your power station from a finite backup into an indefinite power source . With the right panels, you can recharge a 2,000Wh battery in 4–6 hours of good sunlight and keep running critical loads — a fridge, lights, phones, a router — for as long as the sun rises. For an extended outage, that recharge capability is worth more than any extra battery you could buy.
 But here's where it gets confusing: not every solar panel works with every power station. Different brands use different connectors. Voltage limits vary. And a panel that's perfect for car camping might be terrible for home backup . Wattage ratings, cell efficiency, folding designs, weight — there's a lot to sort through.
 We tested and compared the top portable solar panels on the market, focusing on the specs that actually matter: real-world wattage output, connector compatibility, build quality, portability, and value per watt . Below are the five panels we'd pair with our own power stations.

 Monocrystalline: The standard for portable panels. Single-crystal silicon cells deliver the highest efficiency (20–24%) in the smallest footprint. All five of our picks use monocrystalline cells.
 PERC (Passivated Emitter and Rear Cell): An upgrade to standard monocrystalline that adds a reflective layer behind the cells to capture more light. Most premium panels in 2026 use PERC cells, boosting efficiency by 1–2%.
 Bifacial: Panels with transparent backsheets that absorb reflected light from the ground. They can gain 5–15% extra output when placed on light-colored surfaces like concrete, snow, or sand. Increasingly common in rigid rooftop panels but still rare in portable folding designs.
 Portable folding vs. rigid: Folding panels pack down into a briefcase-sized package for transport and unfold to a large surface area for charging. Rigid panels are more durable and slightly more efficient but are bulky and heavy. For pairing with portable power stations, folding panels are almost always the right choice.
 Flexible (thin-film): Ultra-thin panels that can bend and conform to curved surfaces like van roofs or boat decks. Lower efficiency (15–18%) and shorter lifespan than rigid monocrystalline. Best for permanent installations, not portable use.

For DIY battery bank builds, pair any MC4 panel with a Dakota Lithium LiFePO4 battery and an MPPT charge controller.
 Voltage Compatibility: The Spec Most People Miss
 Beyond connectors, you need to check your power station's maximum input voltage (VOC) . Every solar panel has an open-circuit voltage (the voltage it produces when not connected to a load), and this number must be below your station's maximum. Exceeding it can permanently damage the MPPT charge controller.
 BLUETTI AC300: Max VOC 150V — safe with up to 6 panels in series
 EcoFlow Delta Pro: Max VOC 150V — generous headroom for most panel configurations
 EcoFlow Delta 2 Max: Max VOC 60V — be careful wiring panels in series (stick to parallel)
 Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro: Max VOC 45V — only connect 1–2 panels, parallel recommended
 ALLPOWERS R3500: Max VOC 60V — parallel wiring is the safe default
 When in doubt, wire your panels in parallel (positive to positive, negative to negative). This keeps the voltage the same as a single panel while adding amperage, which is almost always within your station's safe input range. For a full breakdown of charging methods and wiring, check our how to charge a solar generator guide .
 Buyer's Guide: How to Choose the Right Solar Panel
 Beyond our specific picks, here's the framework for choosing the right solar panel for your setup.
 How Many Watts Do You Actually Need?
 The rule of thumb is simple: 1W of solar panel capacity for every 5–7Wh of battery capacity . This gives you a full recharge in roughly 5–7 hours of peak sun (accounting for real-world efficiency losses, panel angle, cloud cover, and inverter overhead).
 500Wh power station: 75–100W of panels (one 100W panel)
 1,000Wh power station: 150–200W of panels (one 200W panel)
 2,000Wh power station: 300–400W of panels (two 200W panels or one 400W panel)
 3,000Wh+ power station: 400–800W of panels (two to four 200W panels, or one to two 400W panels)
 You can always add more panels than this formula suggests — up to your station's maximum solar input wattage. More panels mean faster charging, which matters during short winter days or in cloudy climates. You cannot exceed your station's max solar input; the MPPT controller will simply cap intake at its rated maximum.
 Portable Folding vs. Rigid Panels: When to Choose Each
 Portable Folding Panels
 Best for: Camping, tailgating, emergency backup, RV use, apartment balconies. They pack down for storage, weigh 15–35 lbs, and set up in under a minute. All five picks on this list are folding panels. Choose folding if you'll move the panel between locations or store it between uses.
 Rigid Mounted Panels
 Best for: Permanent van/RV roof installations, off-grid cabins, dedicated home backup arrays. Higher efficiency (1–3% more than folding), longer lifespan (25+ years vs. 10–15 for folding), and cheaper per watt. Choose rigid if the panel will stay in one place permanently.
 Bifacial Panels: Worth the Hype?
 Bifacial solar panels have transparent backsheets that allow them to absorb reflected light from the ground surface beneath them. On light-colored surfaces — concrete, white gravel, snow, sand — a bifacial panel can produce 5–15% more power than an equivalent monofacial panel. On dark surfaces like grass or asphalt, the gain drops to 2–5%.
 In 2026, bifacial technology is mainly found in rigid rooftop and ground-mount panels. It's starting to appear in some portable panels, but no current folding panel fully leverages bifacial gains because the panel sits too close to the ground for effective light reflection. If bifacial matters to you, look at rigid panels for a permanent installation.
 Series vs. Parallel Wiring: The Quick Version
 Parallel Wiring (Recommended)
 Positive to positive, negative to negative. Keeps voltage the same, adds amperage. Safer for portable power stations because you won't exceed VOC limits. Use parallel wiring unless your station's manual specifically recommends series. Most power stations include parallel wiring adapters (Y-connectors) in the box.
 Series Wiring (Advanced)
 Positive of panel 1 to negative of panel 2. Adds voltage, keeps amperage the same. Only use series if your station has a high VOC limit (100V+) and you need to minimize cable runs. Warning: if the combined VOC of your panels exceeds your station's max input voltage, you will damage the MPPT controller.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I use any solar panel with any portable power station?
 Not always. Compatibility depends on the connector type and the power station's voltage/amperage input limits. BLUETTI and ALLPOWERS use standard MC4 connectors, so most third-party panels work out of the box. EcoFlow uses a proprietary solar connector (though many panels ship with MC4-to-XT60 adapters). Jackery uses Anderson connectors and works best with their own SolarSaga panels, though MC4-to-Anderson adapters are readily available for $10–$15. Always check your power station's maximum solar input voltage (VOC) before connecting any panel — exceeding the VOC limit can damage the charge controller.
 How many watts of solar panels do I need for my power station?
 A good rule of thumb is 1W of solar panel capacity for every 5–7Wh of battery capacity. For a 1,000Wh power station, aim for 150–200W of panels. For a 2,000Wh unit, 300–400W is ideal. For large 3,000Wh+ systems, 400–800W of solar input will recharge the battery in 4–6 hours of good sun. You can always add more panels later (up to your station's maximum solar input), so starting with one 200W panel and adding a second later is a perfectly valid strategy. Use our solar calculator to dial in the exact numbers for your setup.
 Do portable solar panels work on cloudy days?
 Yes, but at reduced output. On a partly cloudy day, expect 50–70% of rated wattage. On a heavily overcast day, output drops to 15–30%. A 200W panel might produce only 30–60W under thick cloud cover. This is why oversizing your solar array relative to your battery is smart — the extra wattage compensates for imperfect conditions. Monocrystalline panels (all five picks on this list) perform better in low light than polycrystalline alternatives. For more on maximizing solar charging in all conditions, check our charging guide .
 Should I wire solar panels in series or parallel?
 For most portable power stations, parallel wiring is safer and more practical . Parallel keeps the voltage the same while adding amperage — this reduces the risk of exceeding your power station's maximum input voltage (VOC). Series wiring adds voltage together, which can easily exceed your station's VOC limit and damage the MPPT controller. For example, two 200W panels with 24V VOC wired in series produce 48V — which exceeds many stations' 45V limit. The same panels in parallel stay at 24V and double the current. Check your power station's specs before wiring, and when in doubt, go parallel.

 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best solar panel for a portable power station? The EcoFlow NextGen 220W Bifacial. It leads our For power stations score at 8.9 of 10 and has the highest overall Amphourly Score of any panel we track (9.8). It pairs 25% efficient TOPCon cells with IP68 sealing, a built-in adjustable stand and a 21.5 V Voc that fits almost every station's solar input.
 Can I use any solar panel with my power station? Only if the panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) sits inside the station's solar input window and you have the right connector. MC4 panels connect to almost any station with an adapter cable; check the voltage first.
 What happens if my solar panel's wattage is higher than the station's input? Nothing harmful, as long as the voltage fits. The station only draws up to its solar input limit, so the extra watts go unused rather than causing damage.
 Are flexible solar panels worth it? For curved van, boat or RV roofs, yes: the BLUETTI PV100 FX weighs 4.85 lb for 100 W. For a panel you'll set up and pack away, a folding panel's kickstand and higher output are more practical.
 Do I need an MC4 to XT60 adapter? If your panel has MC4 leads and your station has an XT60 or XT60i solar port, yes. Many stations and some panels include one; EcoFlow, for example, includes an XT60i cable with the NextGen 220W.
